name: Lutembacher syndrome
aliases: atrial septal defect with mitral stenosis

clinicalPearls: The combination of an atrial septal defect with mitral stenosis, the latter usually rheumatic and the septal defect most often a secundum type
The mitral stenosis may be congenital or acquired and the atrial defect congenital or, occasionally, iatrogenic after transseptal procedures
The atrial septal defect decompresses the left atrium into the right, so the classic symptoms of mitral stenosis may be muted while right heart and pulmonary features become prominent
The left-to-right shunt is augmented by the raised left atrial pressure of mitral stenosis, increasing right heart volume load and pulmonary blood flow
Auscultation blends the findings of both lesions, and the true diagnosis often rests on echocardiography rather than the physical signs alone
Echocardiography defines the size and severity of both the defect and the valve lesion and guides the treatment strategy
Modern management often combines percutaneous balloon mitral valvuloplasty for suitable valves with device or surgical closure of the atrial septal defect
reference.pathophysiology: In Lutembacher syndrome coexisting mitral stenosis and an atrial septal defect interact haemodynamically. Mitral stenosis obstructs left atrial emptying and raises left atrial pressure; the atrial septal defect then allows this pressurised blood to shunt into the right atrium, so left atrial pressure is partly relieved and the pulmonary venous congestion typical of isolated mitral stenosis may be attenuated. The trade-off is a larger left-to-right shunt than the defect alone would produce, imposing a volume load on the right atrium and ventricle and increasing pulmonary blood flow, which over time can lead to right heart dilatation, atrial arrhythmia, and pulmonary hypertension.
additionalDifferentials: Mitral stenosis with pulmonary hypertension from other causes
Other left-to-right shunts with a mitral inflow lesion
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography to assess mitral valve morphology and gradient and the atrial septal defect
Transoesophageal echocardiography to size the defect and evaluate suitability for closure and valvuloplasty
Assessment of mitral valve suitability for balloon valvuloplasty, including a morphology score
Right heart catheterisation to quantify the shunt and measure pulmonary pressures when needed
Cardiac MRI to quantify shunt volume and right ventricular size in selected cases
redFlags: Progressive right heart failure from combined volume and pressure loading
Development of pulmonary hypertension and shunt reversal
New atrial fibrillation with haemodynamic deterioration or embolic risk
Severe mitral stenosis with a valve unsuitable for balloon valvuloplasty
reference.prognosis: With timely treatment of both the valve lesion and the septal defect the outlook is generally good, but untreated disease can progress to right heart failure, atrial arrhythmia, and pulmonary hypertension.
pitfalls: Missing coexisting mitral stenosis because the atrial defect masks its classic symptoms and signs
Attributing all findings to an isolated atrial septal defect and overlooking the valve lesion
Closing the atrial septal defect without addressing significant mitral stenosis, abruptly raising left atrial pressure
Failing to assess mitral valve suitability before planning balloon valvuloplasty
references: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
ESC Guidelines for the management of adult congenital heart disease
management: Definitive correction of both lesions, combining percutaneous balloon mitral valvuloplasty (or surgical mitral repair or replacement) with device or surgical closure of the atrial septal defect
Diuretics to relieve pulmonary and systemic congestion pending intervention
Rate control and anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation
Secondary antibiotic prophylaxis against rheumatic fever where the mitral stenosis is rheumatic
Serial echocardiography to monitor shunt size, mitral valve gradient, right ventricular function and pulmonary pressures
Manage right heart failure and pulmonary hypertension if the diagnosis is made late
Refer to a cardiology and structural intervention team to plan the combined percutaneous or surgical strategy
